paragraphs: This paper introduces a task that asks where and when sound-producing movements occur in video. Recognizing an action is not enough: the system must locate the particular movement associated with an audible event. The motivating premise is that such events often involve sudden motion changes, as when objects collide.

The proposed architecture, TA²Net, estimates these changes using the second derivative of motion. This provides a visual signal for collision timing without requiring audio input. A second component learns spatial localization through a self-supervised training strategy that combines contrastive learning with spatial analysis. Together, the components address both event timing and the location of the apparent sound source.

The authors also introduce Audible623, a benchmark derived from Kinetics and UCF101 after removing non-essential vocalization subsets. Experiments support the approach on this benchmark and show generalization to repetitive counting and sound source localization. The contribution connects precise action timing with motion dynamics, making sound-associated events identifiable through their visible movement patterns.
icml-2025-action-dubber-timing-audible-a.tldr: TA²Net uses abrupt changes in visible motion to locate sound-producing actions in space and time without audio input.

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks introduce poisoned training examples containing triggers that steer a model toward an attacker’s desired predictions. This paper examines why such attacks can work by studying token selection inside attention. Its goal is to explain a mechanism and establish conditions for success, going beyond empirical demonstrations that an attack happens to work.

The analysis concerns single-head self-attention transformers trained with gradient descent. The authors show that these models can interpolate poisoned training data, meaning they can fit those examples. They then prove successful prediction manipulation when triggers are sufficiently strong without becoming overly dominant. The strength requirement is therefore qualified: the result does not say that any trigger, or an arbitrarily strong one, succeeds.

The theoretical account connects altered outputs to the way an adversary influences which tokens attention selects. Experiments on synthetic datasets validate the findings. This offers a more precise understanding of backdoor vulnerability within the studied architecture and training setting, with the stated trigger conditions forming a central part of the result.
icml-2025-backdoor-attacks-in-token-sele.tldr: The paper explains how backdoor triggers manipulate attention’s token selection and proves attack success under specific trigger-strength conditions.

paragraphs: Autonomous agents need to discover useful behavior while interacting with an environment. Random exploration and slow behavioral updates can make this difficult. This paper proposes learning exploration itself from expert demonstrations, so an agent can use its interaction history to choose purposeful behaviors and adapt online.

Given a dataset of expert demonstrations, the method trains a long-context generative model to predict expert actions. Its inputs include past observations and a measure of how exploratory an expert behavior would be relative to that context. This makes the learning objective sensitive to what the agent has already experienced, rather than treating every expert action as equally informative at every moment.

During deployment, the agent feeds its growing interaction history back into the model. That context lets it select expert behaviors different from those previously chosen, supporting targeted exploration and fast adaptation. Experiments cover simulated locomotion, simulated manipulation, and real robotic manipulation. The findings support learning an adaptive exploration strategy over available expert behaviors, with access to demonstrations central to the approach.
icml-2025-behavioral-exploration-learnin.tldr: Behavioral exploration trains agents to use interaction history to select informative expert-like behaviors and adapt online.

paragraphs: In model-based reinforcement learning, an environment model is useful partly because it supports accurate estimates of future value. Value-aware learning therefore trains models around the value predictions they produce. This paper investigates the theoretical behavior of these objectives, including the MuZero loss, which penalizes disagreement with the ground-truth value function.

The authors show that the usual versions of these losses are uncalibrated surrogate objectives. In this setting, optimizing the training objective does not always recover the correct environment model and value function. This identifies a mismatch between what the loss rewards and what the learning procedure is intended to recover. The paper proposes corrections to address that mismatch.

The analysis also examines how calibration interacts with latent model architectures and auxiliary training losses used in MuZero-style agents. A central distinction is that deterministic models can be sufficient for accurate value prediction, while calibrated stochastic models can still offer advantages. The result motivates choosing training objectives and model architecture together, without claiming that stochastic modeling is necessary for every accurate value estimate.
icml-2025-calibrated-value-aware-model-l.tldr: The paper identifies calibration failures in value-aware model losses and proposes corrections while explaining benefits of calibrated stochastic models.

paragraphs: Graph learning depends on how faithfully a representation captures relationships around each node. Standard graph neural networks aggregate information from nearby nodes, and this process may discard important local details. This paper develops a representation intended to preserve those details while retaining an interpretable connection to the shape of the data.

The starting point is the Euler Characteristic Transform, an efficiently computable representation of global geometric and topological structure. The proposed local version, called ℓ-ECT, applies this perspective to graph neighborhoods. The authors describe it as a lossless representation of those neighborhoods, allowing nuanced local structure to remain available for graph learning. They also construct a rotation-invariant metric from these representations for spatial alignment of data spaces.

On several benchmark node classification tasks, the method outperforms standard graph neural networks. The paper also provides theoretical guarantees for its effectiveness. These contributions bring together local information preservation, geometric comparison, and interpretability, showing how a topology-based representation can improve graph predictions in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-diss-l-ect-dissecting-graph-da.tldr: The local Euler Characteristic Transform preserves graph neighborhood structure and improves benchmark node classification while supporting rotation-invariant comparison.

paragraphs: Learning from demonstrations often produces an agent that imitates a single expert policy. This can restrict the variety of behaviors available when conditions change. The paper introduces Quality Diversity Inverse Reinforcement Learning, a framework for learning a collection of useful behaviors from limited demonstrations by combining inverse reinforcement learning with quality-diversity optimization.

Its central mechanism is Extrinsic Behavioral Curiosity. An external critic gives additional rewards according to how novel a behavior is relative to a large archive of behaviors. The archive supplies a reference for diversity, while the surrounding learning framework maintains the connection to demonstrated behavior and performance. This makes behavioral novelty an explicit training signal.

Across the included robot locomotion environments, curiosity improves framework instances using GAIL, VAIL, and DiffAIL, with reported gains reaching 185%, 42%, and 150%, respectively. The method also exceeds expert performance by 20% on Humanoid. Further experiments show applicability to Gradient-Arborescence-based quality-diversity reinforcement learning, extending the mechanism beyond the imitation-based framework and supporting its usefulness for learning varied policies.
icml-2025-diversifying-policy-behaviors-.tldr: An external curiosity critic rewards novelty against a behavioral archive, improving the diversity and performance of learned robot policies.

paragraphs: Epidemic forecasting must account for both changing infection trends and the mechanisms that move disease between regions. This paper proposes EARTH, an end-to-end forecasting framework designed to incorporate those features. Its approach connects continuous epidemic evolution with regional transmission patterns and broader infection trends.

The first component, EANO, combines a neural ordinary differential equation approach with an epidemic mechanism. It learns regional transmission while accounting for spatial spread over time. A second component, GLTG, models global infection trends and uses them to guide local transmission dynamically. These components represent complementary information: the overall direction of an epidemic and the details of how it develops locally.

EARTH uses cross-attention to combine meaningful information from the two components for forecasting. This allows global coherence and local variation to contribute to the same prediction process. Experiments on real-world epidemics report better forecasting performance than state-of-the-art methods. The findings support incorporating disease transmission mechanisms and multiple spatial scales into learned forecasts within the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-earth-epidemiology-aware-neura.tldr: EARTH combines continuous regional transmission modeling with global infection trends to improve epidemic forecasting.

paragraphs: Flow matching generates samples by following a learned vector field through an ordinary differential equation. This paper studies how those trajectories relate to the geometry of the underlying data. Understanding that relationship helps explain where generated samples move and how the sampling process behaves near its endpoint.

The analysis centers on the denoiser, which guides trajectories through attracting and absorbing behaviors that reflect data geometry. The authors distinguish three stages of evolution. During the initial and intermediate stages, trajectories move toward the data mean and local clusters. At the terminal stage, they establish convergence under weak assumptions, including situations where the data occupy a low-dimensional submanifold.

Handling such low-dimensional structure extends beyond cases covered by earlier results. The terminal analysis also provides insight into memorization and establishes equivariance properties, describing how the dynamics relate to transformations. The contribution is principally theoretical: it connects sampling behavior with data geometry and provides a basis for geometry-informed choices of sampling strategies and model architectures.
icml-2025-elucidating-flow-matching-ode-.tldr: The paper explains flow-matching trajectories through denoiser behavior and proves terminal convergence under weak assumptions, including low-dimensional data settings.

paragraphs: Many denoising methods benefit from the fact that clean signals have low-dimensional structure even when their recorded representation is large. This paper studies how to denoise a new observation when that structure is an unknown manifold and only noisy samples are available. The goal is efficient denoising at test time.

The proposed framework treats learning to denoise as learning an optimization procedure over the manifold of clean signals. Online learning grows this optimizer incrementally, using one noisy sample at a time. Mixed-order methods provide guarantees that the learned optimizers reach global optimality, supporting efficient computation together with near-optimal denoising performance in the paper’s analysis.

The authors analyze both the computational complexity and denoising performance of mixed-order traversal. Experiments on scientific manifolds show improved tradeoffs between computational cost and denoising quality compared with nearest neighbor search. This matters because exhaustive nearest neighbor search supports existing provable approaches but requires searching the dataset. The proposed framework instead makes the learned optimization procedure central to processing new noisy observations.
icml-2025-fast-accurate-manifold-denoisi.tldr: The method learns a manifold optimizer from noisy samples to achieve efficient, theoretically supported denoising at test time.

paragraphs: When some inputs are missing, asking which features matter can refer to different questions. This paper separates importance in a hypothetical fully measured dataset from importance under the measurements actually available. The latter depends on the current measurement policy, which determines what information reaches the model.

The full-data perspective can reveal aspects of the data-generating process, but it often requires unrealistic assumptions. It also cannot guide decisions when missingness continues during deployment. Observed-data importance addresses the actual measurement setting, yet neither perspective directly answers which features should be collected more often to improve predictions. That distinction separates interpretation from decisions about data collection.

To address the collection question, the authors introduce the feature measurement importance gradient, or FMIG. This model-agnostic metric identifies features whose more frequent measurement would enhance predictive performance. Synthetic-data examples illustrate how the metrics differ and why treating them as interchangeable can be misleading. The contribution is a clearer match between the question being asked and the feature-importance quantity used to answer it.
icml-2025-feature-importance-metrics-in-.tldr: The paper distinguishes feature importance under missing data from the value of measuring a feature more often, introducing FMIG for the latter.

paragraphs: One-shot subset selection reduces training costs by choosing an informative portion of a dataset before training. The selection depends on an information extractor, often a model previously trained on the target dataset. This paper investigates whether foundation models can provide a less dataset-dependent alternative and whether their usefulness varies across models.

The experiments reveal that the advantage depends on the dataset. Foundation models consistently outperform traditional information extractors on fine-grained datasets, where categories require detailed distinctions. Their advantage becomes smaller on coarse-grained datasets with noisy labels. These findings motivate a method specifically aimed at fine-grained image selection rather than an assumption that foundation models offer the same benefit everywhere.

The proposed RAM-APL method, short for RAnking Mean-Accuracy of Pseudo-class Labels, combines multiple foundation models to use their complementary strengths. It achieves state-of-the-art results on fine-grained datasets including Oxford-IIIT Pet, Food-101, and Caltech-UCSD Birds-200-2011. The contribution links an empirical investigation of information extractors to a selection strategy tailored to the setting where their benefits are strongest.
icml-2025-foundation-model-insights-and-.tldr: RAM-APL combines complementary foundation models to improve one-shot subset selection for fine-grained image datasets.

paragraphs: Next-token language generation cannot revise tokens it has already produced. Discrete diffusion offers an alternative, but the popular masked version reintroduces this restriction. This paper generalizes masked diffusion to make the underlying noising process more flexible, creating a family called general interpolating discrete diffusion, or GIDD.

The authors derive a new diffusion evidence lower bound, a training objective that supports this broader family. With this objective, they report compute-matched state-of-the-art performance in diffusion language modeling. Matching computation matters to the stated comparison because the reported result concerns performance at a comparable computational budget.

The paper then uses GIDD’s flexibility to combine masking with uniform noise. This hybrid improves generated sample quality and allows the model to correct its own mistakes. The contribution therefore connects the design of the corruption process to the behavior available during generation: changing how tokens are noised enables a generation process that can revisit earlier choices. The reported findings concern this hybrid approach and the evaluated diffusion language-modeling setting.
icml-2025-generalized-interpolating-disc.tldr: GIDD generalizes discrete diffusion, using flexible noise processes to improve language generation and enable correction of earlier token choices.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can generate pseudolabels to help adapt themselves to downstream tasks. These predicted labels often favor some categories over others, creating an imbalance that harms performance. This paper investigates the causes of that imbalance and develops a framework intended to improve both label accuracy and coverage across classes.

The authors identify two primary contributing factors: concept mismatch and concept confusion. Their framework pairs concept alignment with a confusion-aware calibrated margin mechanism to address these issues. The stated focus is to strengthen underperforming classes and encourage more balanced predictions across categories, connecting the correction strategy to the diagnosed sources of imbalance.

Experiments span six benchmark datasets and three learning paradigms. The method improves the accuracy and balance of pseudolabels and reports a 6.29% relative improvement over the state-of-the-art method. This is a relative gain, rather than a stated percentage-point increase. The findings support addressing how concepts align and become confused when using model-generated labels for adaptation, with evidence across the evaluated datasets and learning settings.
icml-2025-handling-imbalanced-pseudolabe.tldr: Concept alignment and confusion-aware margins improve the accuracy and class balance of vision-language-model pseudolabels.

paragraphs: Choosing AdamW’s weight decay becomes difficult when model and dataset sizes change. This paper interprets the learned weights as an exponential moving average of recent updates. That view shifts attention to the averaging timescale: roughly, how many recent training iterations contribute to the weights.

The authors find that the optimal timescale, expressed in epochs, stays approximately constant as model and dataset sizes vary. For a given learning rate, the timescale maps one-to-one to weight decay. If the optimal timescale remains constant, increasing dataset size implies decreasing weight decay. Increasing model size implies increasing weight decay when the learning rate follows the muP scaling recommendation.

The paper validates these rules using ResNet-18 and Vision Transformers on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, plus NanoGPT pre-training on OpenWebText. It also finds that muP learning-rate scaling breaks down later in AdamW training unless weight decay is adjusted appropriately. The practical contribution is a connected account of learning rate, decay, and training timescale, with the proposed scaling directions resting on the approximately constant-timescale finding.
icml-2025-how-to-set-adamws-weight-decay.tldr: Viewing AdamW weights as an exponential moving average yields conditional weight-decay scaling rules for larger datasets and models.

paragraphs: Continuous image representations can encode shapes, colors, and textures without storing them solely as a fixed pixel grid. Conventional implicit neural representations map coordinates to colors through a neural network. GaussianImage instead uses Gaussian functions, achieving similar quality and compression, but the paper identifies its lack of image modification as a limitation.

MiraGe introduces a representation designed for editing. It uses mirror reflections to perceive a two-dimensional image in three-dimensional space and represents it with flat-controlled Gaussians. This construction supports precise image changes while improving rendering quality. Modeling the image in three dimensions also creates the visual illusion of edits based on three-dimensional structure.

The authors show that the Gaussian representation can be combined with a physics engine to produce physics-based modifications of two-dimensional images. They report better quality than the standard approach alongside natural-looking editing capabilities. The contribution joins image representation and manipulation: the same representation that produces the rendered image also supplies a structure for visually plausible modifications.
icml-2025-mirage-editable-2d-images-usin.tldr: MiraGe represents 2D images with controlled Gaussians in 3D space to improve rendering and enable natural, physics-based edits.

paragraphs: Pipeline parallelism distributes large-model training across stages, but storing activations can limit its scalability. As the pipeline grows, more microbatches remain in flight, increasing the associated memory demand. This paper studies memory offloading as a way to reduce that pressure while preserving useful training throughput.

An empirical study finds that, in most standard configurations examined, at least half of the activations—and potentially all of them—can be offloaded with negligible overhead. When complete offloading is not possible, the authors propose a selective strategy that reduces peak activation memory in a better-than-linear manner. They also combine offloading with other techniques to jointly account for memory limits and throughput.

In the experiments, activation memory per device decreases as the total number of stages increases. The resulting pipeline approach offers acceleration of up to 19% over tensor parallelism while using less memory. These results show how managing activation storage can change the practical scaling behavior of pipeline training, with the extent of inexpensive offloading dependent on the configuration.
icml-2025-pipeoffload-improving-scalabil.tldr: PipeOffload reduces pipeline-training activation memory through offloading, achieving up to 19% acceleration over tensor parallelism in the experiments.

paragraphs: Incremental learning requires acquiring new tasks without catastrophically forgetting earlier ones. Parameter-isolation methods address this by assigning task-specific subsets of a network’s parameters through masks. This paper argues that existing approaches often overlook dependencies among parameters, which can make them rely too heavily on newly allocated parameters.

Probabilistic Group Mask selection, or PGM, makes those dependencies part of mask selection. It divides parameters into groups, supplies multiple candidate masks within each group, and assigns probabilities to the candidates. Gumbel-Softmax enables differentiable sampling, allowing the discrete choice of masks to be optimized efficiently through the training process.

The authors provide theoretical analysis showing that incorporating parameter dependencies improves subnetwork selection. Experiments on standard incremental-learning benchmarks also find the method more effective than existing approaches. The contribution is to treat a task’s parameter allocation as a coordinated selection problem: choosing useful combinations within groups can account for relationships that would be missed when parameter choices disregard their dependencies.
icml-2025-probabilistic-group-mask-guide.tldr: PGM improves incremental learning by selecting parameter masks in groups that account for dependencies among parameters.

paragraphs: Graph ordinary differential equations model systems whose components interact as they evolve. With limited observational training data, their predictions can generalize poorly. This paper identifies two causes: initialization mixes static attributes with changing states, and training encourages reliance on coupling patterns specific to the observed context.

The proposed GREAT framework uses a structural causal model to analyze misleading dependence paths. Its Dynamic-Static Equilibrium Decoupler separates static and dynamic information through projections into orthogonal subspaces, supporting robust initialization. Its Causal Mediation for Coupled Dynamics module uses variational inference to estimate latent causal factors, aiming to reduce spurious correlations and learn coupling dynamics that transfer more broadly.

Experiments across diverse dynamical systems report better results than state-of-the-art methods both within and outside the training distribution. The findings support treating initialization and interaction modeling as connected sources of generalization failure. GREAT addresses both through disentanglement and regularization, with the reported evidence showing improved transfer across the evaluated system settings rather than establishing success in every unseen situation.
icml-2025-rethink-graphode-generalizatio.tldr: GREAT improves GraphODE generalization by separating static and dynamic information and reducing reliance on context-specific coupling patterns.

paragraphs: Online distributed optimization lets multiple networked agents learn from data as it arrives. The problem becomes more challenging when valid solutions lie on a Riemannian manifold, a space with geometric constraints. An algorithm must accommodate that geometry while remaining efficient and able to adapt continuously to streaming observations.

This paper develops a diffusion adaptation strategy for decentralized optimization over general manifolds. The strategy addresses learning across a network without relying on a centralized optimization arrangement. Its theoretical analysis shows that, after enough iterations, the agents can approach agreement. That agreement property then supports a non-asymptotic convergence result, giving a statement about convergence at finite iteration counts.

The authors apply the algorithm to online decentralized principal component analysis and Gaussian mixture model inference. Experiments using both synthetic and real data illustrate its performance. The contribution brings geometric constraints, network coordination, and ongoing adaptation into one optimization framework, supported by convergence analysis and applications to two learning problems. The agreement claim concerns approaching consensus after sufficient iterations.
icml-2025-riemannian-diffusion-adaptatio.tldr: A decentralized diffusion strategy supports online optimization on manifolds, with network-agreement analysis and finite-iteration convergence results.

paragraphs: Sparse linear systems appear throughout scientific computing, including partial differential equations and computer vision. Making their solvers useful inside neural networks requires both computational efficiency and reliable differentiation. This paper targets direct sparse solvers, whose computational cost has restricted their adoption as components of neural architectures.

The method condenses a sparse Laplacian matrix into a dense tensor containing batches of smaller Dirichlet-to-Neumann matrices. Solving the original system then becomes a recursive process of merging pairs of these smaller dense matrices. The resulting systems are sliced and inverted in parallel, allowing the computation to use highly optimized dense GPU linear-algebra kernels.

The authors report acceleration of up to three orders of magnitude for direct sparse solving. They also present the method as a strong zero-shot baseline for AI-based PDE solving and as a reliable differentiable component for machine-learning pipelines. The central computational idea is to reorganize a sparse problem into batches of small dense operations, aligning the solver’s workload with operations that GPUs execute efficiently.
icml-2025-schwarzschur-involution-lights.tldr: The solver reorganizes sparse Laplacian systems into small batched dense operations, reporting speedups of up to three orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Language models can have complementary strengths because their training equips them differently across domains. This paper proposes combining that knowledge during generation, without additional training of the language models. The aim is to improve answers while keeping collaboration efficient enough to be useful at inference time.

Collaborative Speculative Decoding, or CoSD, begins with a draft model that generates initial sequences. An easy-to-learn rule or decision tree determines when an assistant model should be called to improve those drafts. This selection mechanism makes the decision to collaborate explicit and interpretable, while the draft-and-assistant structure provides a way to combine knowledge during decoding.

Experiments report accuracy improvements of up to 10% over existing methods across benchmarks, alongside improved inference efficiency. The authors also report transferability across domains and greater explainability. The contribution places collaboration inside the generation procedure itself: the system decides when another model’s knowledge is useful for a draft. The stated benefit therefore includes both stronger predictions and a practical mechanism for managing model cooperation.
icml-2025-speculate-then-collaborate-fus.tldr: CoSD selectively calls an assistant model to improve draft generations, combining model knowledge efficiently without further language-model training.

paragraphs: Optimal transport provides ways to compare distributions, but high dimensionality makes those comparisons difficult. Kernel max-sliced Wasserstein distance addresses this by finding an optimal nonlinear mapping into one dimension before computing a Wasserstein distance. This paper investigates the statistical reliability and computational difficulty of that construction.

The authors establish sharp finite-sample guarantees for the KMS p-Wasserstein distance between empirical distributions with n samples, covering finite p values from one upward. These results use milder technical assumptions than previous state-of-the-art guarantees. They clarify what can be established when the distance is computed from a finite amount of data.

On the computational side, the paper proves that computing the KMS 2-Wasserstein distance is NP-hard. It then develops a semidefinite relaxation that can be solved in polynomial time and provides a relaxation-gap result. Numerical examples show good performance for high-dimensional two-sample testing. Together, the contributions distinguish reliable statistical estimation from difficult exact optimization and offer an efficiently solvable approximation with theoretical characterization.
icml-2025-statistical-and-computational-.tldr: The paper establishes statistical guarantees for KMS Wasserstein distances and offers a tractable relaxation of their NP-hard computation for p = 2.

paragraphs: Large industrial decision problems expose different weaknesses in language models and reinforcement learning. Language models struggle with real-time decisions across long sequences, while reinforcement learning can require many samples when the action space is vast. Agents Co-Evolution, or ACE, connects the two approaches so each can improve the other during training.

The language model takes two roles in refining reinforcement-learning trajectories. As a Policy Actor, it uses multi-step reasoning and environment validation to improve suboptimal actions. As a Value Critic, it shapes rewards across a trajectory to help assign credit over time. In the other direction, prioritized experience replay from the reinforcement-learning agent improves the language model’s task-specific decision-making.

Experiments evaluate ACE on several power-grid operation challenges with more than 60,000 discrete actions. The framework outperforms existing reinforcement-learning and language-model-based methods in these evaluations. The contribution is a reciprocal training process: reasoning and trajectory-level feedback support the reinforcement-learning agent, while selected experience supports the language model’s decisions in the same task setting.
icml-2025-think-twice-act-once-a-co-evol.tldr: ACE lets language models refine reinforcement-learning trajectories while prioritized experience improves the language models’ task-specific decisions.

paragraphs: Models that align images and text can be disrupted by adversarial inputs. This paper studies those disruptions through the topology of image and text embeddings: the structural patterns formed by their representations. The authors find that attacks disturb cross-modal alignment in ways that leave distinctive topological signatures.

Using persistent homology, they introduce two Topological-Contrastive losses based on Total Persistence and multi-scale kernel methods. Across a wide range of attacks, these losses show monotonic changes as the data contain more adversarial samples. This observed pattern connects the amount of adversarial contamination with a measurable change in the structure of the aligned representations.

The authors then design an algorithm that back-propagates these signatures to input samples and incorporates them into Maximum Mean Discrepancy tests. The resulting tests use topological information to improve adversarial detection. The contribution moves from identifying structural effects of attacks to making those effects useful in a detection procedure, with the monotonic behavior supported by observations across the attacks studied.
icml-2025-topological-signatures-of-adve.tldr: Topological changes in image-text embeddings provide signatures of adversarial attacks that improve statistical detection.

paragraphs: Continual learning requires learning new tasks while retaining earlier knowledge. This paper studies forgetting through feature learning, asking how relationships between task signals affect that process. Its theoretical setting uses sequential tasks from a signal-noise data model and a two-layer convolutional network with polynomial ReLU activation.

Within this setting, the angle between task signal vectors separates different forgetting behaviors. Acute angles and small obtuse angles lead to benign forgetting, whereas larger obtuse angles lead to harmful forgetting. The analysis also shows that replaying earlier examples expands the range of angles associated with benign forgetting. Replay therefore changes which task relationships the learner can accommodate favorably.

These results motivate mid-angle sampling, which chooses replay examples whose angles to a prototype are moderate. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical findings and show the effectiveness of this sampling strategy. The contribution connects a geometric account of task interaction with a concrete replay-selection method, while the formal angle-based conclusions are established in the specified network and data model.
icml-2025-understanding-the-forgetting-o.tldr: A feature-learning analysis links forgetting to task-signal angles and motivates selecting moderate-angle examples for replay.
